direct.prompt: Can one number stand in the relation 'is a tarn-divisor of' to another without being a fen-divisor of it?

chain: 6 is a fen-divisor of 42. (given in prompt)
'Is a tarn-divisor of' is a subproperty of 'is a fen-divisor of'. (edit)
The subproperty runs from tarn to fen only, so tarn does not follow from fen: no.

derived.prompt: 6 is a tarn-divisor of 42. Does it follow that 6 is a fen-divisor of 42?
chain: 6 is a tarn-divisor of 42. (given in prompt)
'Is a tarn-divisor of' is a subproperty of 'is a fen-divisor of'. (edit)
So 6 is a fen-divisor of 42: yes.

'Is a tarn-divisor of' is a subproperty.why: Two made-up relations between numbers, one placed under the other. Both absent from Dolma and from a web search.

sources.note: None of the three phrases is used anywhere; hits were stent grafts and graph-theory "grafts".

notes: Fictional relations (both made up, so the subproperty is not a real fact that would hold anyway), real instances (6 and 42). Direct no (asked as 'tarn without fen?'), d1 no (the converse), d2 yes. Near query: a real subproperty (largest prime factor ⊑ prime factor). RBox: the instance facts are in the prompt, so each 'Does it follow ...?' query is determinate by construction (no determinacy, no worlds). A 'no' answer (the conclusion does not follow) is the same before and after the insert, since nothing follows about a made-up relation before it, so those queries carry discriminates: false; they are there to keep yes and no balanced (CRITERIA Rule 9) and to catch over-generalization of the inserted property. Locality references are the logical answers; the scoring gold is the model's own pre-edit answer.
